# Voice profile — eff-mullin

## 1. Cadence

The default sentence is medium-length and declarative. The prose moves through legal analysis without a columnist's drama but with more cut than a legal brief. The sharpest move is the short sentence dropped after a build: in `kids-online-safety-act-will-make-internet-worse-everyone`, *"When the safest legal option is to delete a forum, platforms will delete the forum"* appears twice, once mid-piece and once at section close — a hammer used twice. In `californias-ab-412-still-demands-developers-do-impossible`, a paragraph establishing a premise ends: *"That simply isn't true."* Three words. If a paragraph has been building through several clauses, end it on its shortest sentence — one clause, subject-verb or subject-verb-object.

Parentheticals interrupt constantly throughout all 11 samples — 97 instances, 12.03 per 1,000 words ([measurement:round-parenthetical-spans]) — carrying bill citations, definitions, and mid-clause qualifications without breaking the main sentence. Em-dashes do similar work, 53 instances, 6.57 per 1,000 words ([measurement:em-dashes]), in 10/11 samples, several times per piece. Neither marks a major rhetorical shift; both mark a quick aside before the clause continues.

## 2. How a piece opens

9/11 samples open with the bill's name and current status in the first sentence, then immediately disrupt the bill's official self-description. `congress-just-rushed-through-disastrous-copyright-office-overhaul`: *"In a voice vote earlier this week, the House of Representatives passed H.R. 6028, the 'Legislative Branch Agencies Clarification Act.'"* Second sentence: *"The legislation is presented as a technical reorganization of some government agencies, but it's much more than that."* The pattern is: name the thing, then correct what the thing claims to be. No scene-setting, no anecdote, no wind-up. If the bill claims to do X, the rebuttal arrives by sentence three at the latest.

## 3. How a piece closes

10/11 samples end with a direct statement of what should happen — a named institution addressed by name (*"The Senate should reject H.R. 6028"*) or a flat verdict (*"KOSA will not make kids safer. It will make the internet more dangerous"*). The final sentence is the shortest in the closing paragraph and is never a question. Where a reader call-to-action link appears, the verdict follows it — the last word belongs to the argument, not the link.

## 4. Who is being addressed, and how

The dominant pronoun is *we*, carrying EFF and often the reader as a shared public — [measurement:first-person-plural-family] 19 instances, 2.36 per 1,000 words, 10/11 samples, throughout pieces that contain it. This *we* sometimes narrows to EFF specifically (*"EFF opposed this bill from the start"*), but the framing positions issues as shared stakes, not EFF-versus-everyone.

*You* is sparse — [measurement:second-person-family] 11 instances, 1.36 per 1,000 words, 5/11 samples, once or twice per piece when it appears — and almost entirely confined to paragraphs telling California residents how to contact their legislators. Outside those call-to-action closers, the reader is a member of the concerned public, not an individual being instructed. Use *you* only where you are literally directing a specific reader to take a specific action.

First-person singular is near-absent: [measurement:first-person-singular-family] 2 instances, 0.25 per 1,000 words, 2/11 samples — 1/10 of the rate of *we*. The writer does not appear as a person with a history or views; the argument is carried by collective voice and by the record. Do not introduce *I* except inside a direct quotation from a letter. Use *we*.

Contractions run throughout every piece — [measurement:contractions] 86 instances, 10.66 per 1,000 words, 11/11 samples. Against them, uncontracted negatives (*do not*, *cannot*, *will not*, *is not*) appear at [measurement:uncontracted-negatives] 32 instances, 3.97 per 1,000 words, 9/11 samples. Contractions outnumber uncontracted negatives by more than two and a half to one; the uncontracted forms carry extra formality or emphasis when they appear. When in doubt, contract.

Questions appear [measurement:question-marks] 9 instances, 1.12 per 1,000 words, 4/11 samples — once or twice per piece, never several times — and function as framing moves: a question names the problem, the following paragraph answers it. Direct questions to the reader are rare.

Named opponents and named allies both appear throughout 8/11 samples. Opponents are named precisely — specific bill sponsors, specific companies, *Big Tech* as a collective — and the critique is directed at their actions, not their character. Allies are named as coalition members, cited by organisation. The argument is made by EFF and supported by the record; it is not made through extended quotation of outside authorities.

## 5. Figures

Figures are short, pointed, and not elaborated — 8/11 samples. The typical move is a vivid noun phrase embedded in analytical prose and dropped without commentary: *"a death sentence"* for small-startup compliance burdens (`californias-ab-412-bill-could-crush-startups`), *"heckler's veto"* for takedown incentives (`no-fakes-act-could-silence-satire`), *"smokescreen"* for a bill's claimed carveout (`kids-online-safety-act`), *"card catalog"* for the copyright registration system. Each figure names a problem vividly and the analysis moves on. No figure is reopened or extended.

No rate is possible: "a pointed noun phrase" cannot be enumerated reproducibly. What can be said about the vocabulary: concrete nouns from everyday life and bureaucratic reality — catalogs, vaults, death sentences, gift — not abstractions. When you reach for a figure, reach into that register and drop it in one clause.

## 6. Register range

The register is consistent across all 11 samples regardless of length. Subheadings appear in 8/11 samples and are declarative statements of position — *"This Bill Was Rushed Through"*, *"A Burden That Can't Be Met"* — not neutral labels. Use declarative headings that carry the argument when writing pieces of more than 500 words. When stakes are highest, the short-sentence move becomes more frequent; the vocabulary stays formal throughout, and intensity is carried by precision and the punchy sentence, not by adjective accumulation.

## 7. What the corpus never does

Profanity is absent — [measurement:profanity-vulgarity] 0 instances, 11/11 samples. The register's informality is carried instead by contractions (86 instances, 10.66 per 1,000 words, [measurement:contractions]), which appear throughout every piece. Do not introduce profanity.

Extended anecdote or scene-setting does not appear in any of the 11 samples. The positive habit occupying its place: pieces open directly on the legislative situation and name the stakes in the first three sentences (`california-ab-412-stalls-out-win-innovation-and-fair-use`: *"A.B. 412, the flawed California bill that threatened small developers in the name of AI 'transparency,' has been delayed"*). Where a concrete example appears it is named briefly and its legal significance is stated immediately. Do not open with a story.

## 8. What this profile could not determine

**Voice card:** Unfilled. All observations are derived from the corpus alone.

**Qualification and hedging:** Hedging phrases appear (*"at a minimum"*, *"in most of the AI cases"*, *"at least"*) but no stable countable form was identified. The habit exists; its rate cannot be honestly stated.

**Opponents, allies, and sources:** Named opponents and allies appear in 8/11 samples but "naming an opponent" is a judgment call, not a grammatical form. The pattern is described qualitatively in section 4; no rate is given.

**Profanity pairing:** The absence of profanity (0 instances) is established by measurement. The pairing in the coverage record uses contractions as the positive — the register's informality carrier — which is the closest countable counterpart available, not a perfect functional equivalent.

**Register toward different audiences:** All 11 samples address a general technology-policy readership. How this voice behaves toward a purely legal or purely technical audience cannot be determined from this corpus.

**Observations dropped:** 3 — one on sentence-length averages (not supported by a reproducible count), one on frequency of hyperlinked citations (could not separate authorial from edited link placement reliably), one on modal verbs as hedges (pattern inconsistent across samples).
